strengths: The paper proposes a coherent bilevel architecture that separates high-level LLM task decisions from low-level toolchain execution, with a four-action decision space (direct response, clarification, toolchain retrieval, execution) covering common interaction modes.

The Tool World Navigation Model (TWNM) is a substantive idea: it builds a directed weighted graph with structural and behavioral edges from execution traces, uses a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer for link prediction with edge-weight-aware attention, and supports dynamic evolution via node integration, subgraph pruning, and edge attribute propagation.

The method includes a failure-recovery mechanism (path recombination) and reports ablations over agent-only, static graph, dynamic graph, and alpha-beta vs heuristic search, which is a useful decomposition of the contribution.

Experiments span multiple foundation models (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1-32B) and task difficulties, with TSR/TCR/Steps metrics; the reported trends generally favor NaviAgent over ReAct, ToolLLM, and α-UMI.
The appendix provides implementation details, prompts, algorithm pseudocode, and case studies, showing effort toward transparency and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims rest on a simulated API environment rather than real API execution. The paper states real-time API execution is unavailable, and evaluation uses an LLM-based API simulator plus a GPT-4.1 judge. This weakens the validity of the reported task success rates and makes the 'best task success rates' claim unsupported in real-world settings.

The API simulator has an internal contradiction: for error cases it says to set {'status': 'success', 'type': 'error'}, so failures are not surfaced as failures. This undermines evaluation of the closed-loop failure recovery and path recombination mechanisms, which are key claimed contributions.

There is an inconsistency between the main text's claim that real-time API execution is unavailable and Appendix F.1's claim of 'real-world evaluations on 50 APIs from RapidAPI' (only 60 queries). This raises concerns about the evaluation protocol and reproducibility.

The evaluation benchmark is newly generated from API dependency trees using LLM prompts, not the standard ToolBench/API-Bank evaluation protocols. Sample sizes, generation distributions, and public release of the generated data/code are not provided, so others cannot reliably reproduce or compare results.

Baseline fairness is questionable: NaviAgent includes a supervised fine-tuned Qwen2.5-14B variant, while baselines are not fine-tuned; main results omit some models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1-32B) that appear elsewhere, and key graph-based methods discussed in related work (ToolNet, ControlLLM, ToolChain*, ToolPlanner, Confucius) are not compared.

The ablation evidence for the dynamic graph is mixed: improvements over the static graph are small on many hard settings (e.g., Qwen2.5-32B Hard TSR 26.3 vs 31.4; GPT-4o Hard 37.9 vs 41.4; DeepSeek-V3 Hard 31.1 vs 33.3), and heuristic search sometimes decreases hard-task TSR (Qwen2.5-32B Dynamic+H 30.8 vs Dynamic+A 31.4). The claim that heuristic search adds '2-3 points on all tasks and about 8 points on hard cases' is not consistently supported by Table 2.
The four-dimensional decision space is not ablated action-by-action; Figure 5 gives only qualitative proportions. There is no evidence isolating the benefit of clarification or re-retrieval actions.

The 'bilevel' and 'closed-loop optimization' claims are not formalized: no bilevel optimization problem is solved, and the policy update from execution feedback is not specified beyond offline SFT and graph edge updates. The paper does not demonstrate online policy adaptation.

Technical details are insufficient: graph construction and parameter standardization are only briefly described; HGT hyperparameters, negative sampling size k, margin m0, loss weights μ0 and γ, and training data composition are missing. The graph search uses many hand-tuned parameters (α0=0.4, β0=0.9, fitness weights, annealing schedule) without sensitivity analysis.

Link prediction is evaluated only with ACC/F1/AUC in Table 8 (AUC 0.75 and 0.71) and without comparison to baselines (e.g., MLP, other GNNs), so it is unclear whether the HGT component actually improves tool dependency modeling.

Metrics rely on an LLM judge for TSR with no human validation, inter-annotator agreement, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Steps are counted only for successful tasks, which can bias efficiency comparisons.
Reproducibility is limited: no code, data, model checkpoints, or compute details are released; the API simulator, generated tasks, and evaluation prompts are not enough to recreate the full pipeline.

Presentation has multiple issues: inconsistent acronyms (TWMN vs TWNM), typos ('TooChain', 'the our framework', 'Deepseek' capitalization), broken/ambiguous appendix formatting, and low-resolution figures. A limitations and broader-impact section is largely absent.
Ethical and risk considerations are not discussed: using simulated APIs and fabricated outputs could mislead downstream use, and there is no discussion of tool misuse, licensing, or safety risks.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem (scaling LLM function-calling agents to large, evolving tool ecosystems) with a plausible graph-based formulation.

The bilevel decomposition (decision agent + Tool World Navigation Model) is conceptually clean, and the four-dimensional action space (direct response / clarification / toolchain retrieval / tool execution) is a sensible design for covering interaction scenarios.

Experiments span several foundation models (open and closed source) and two benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank), and the ablation in Table 2 isolates static vs. dynamic graphs and alpha-beta vs. heuristic search, which is a useful breakdown.
Appendix F adds a real-world API test on 50 RapidAPI endpoints and a runtime analysis, and the SFT finding (Qwen2.5-14B approaching the 32B model) is practically interesting.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is not trustworthy. Section 4.1 states 'real-time API execution is currently unavailable,' so all main results come from an author-built simulator whose responses are produced by an LLM prompt ('API Chain Simulator,' Appendix E.3.3). Task success is therefore judged against a simulator the authors control, which can bias results in favor of the proposed method and makes the headline TSR/TCR numbers (Tables 1-2, 7) hard to interpret.

Task construction (Appendix D) builds problems around API dependency chains — precisely the structure TWNM exploits — and is itself LLM-generated. This creates a plausible bias/leakage risk favoring the proposed graph method; the claim of 'strict separation between fine-tuning and evaluation data' (Section 4.1) is asserted but not substantiated (no decontamination procedure or overlap analysis).

The closest prior work on graph-based tool orchestration is only cited, never compared. ToolNet [5], ControlLLM [24], ToolPlanner [7], and ToolChain* [23] are the most relevant baselines for the exact problem being addressed, yet the empirical comparison is limited to ReAct, ToolLLM, and α-UMI. Without these comparisons the claimed superiority over 'static graphs' is unsupported.

Baselines appear under-tuned. ReAct reaches only ~20-30% TSR across models (Table 1), which is far below typical reported ReAct tool-use performance, and no evidence is given that baselines received comparable tool-retrieval, prompting, or retry budgets. This makes the reported gaps difficult to attribute to the proposed architecture.

No variance or statistical reporting: all results appear to be single runs with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, yet the paper makes strong 'best across models and tasks' and 'up to 17 points' claims (Abstract). The 17-point figure is also not clearly traceable in the tables (hard-task gains vary widely, e.g., +13.8 on Deepseek-V3 vs. +20.5 on GPT-4o), suggesting selective reporting.

Limited methodological novelty. The components are largely standard: heterogeneous graph transformer link prediction [27-29], alpha-beta pruning [36], simulated-annealing/genetic search [37, 38], and standard SFT (Eq. 3). The 'bilevel' framing is mostly conceptual, and the four-dimensional decision space is essentially a prompt specification (Appendix E.3.1) rather than a new learning mechanism.

The scalability claim ('thousands of tools,' Abstract/Intro) is not empirically demonstrated. While ToolBench contains ~5501 APIs (Table 8), the actual scale used at evaluation and the behavior of retrieval/search at that scale (latency, recall, path quality) are not reported, so the core scaling claim is unvalidated.

Efficiency claims conflict with the authors' own runtime data. Table 6 shows Dynamic+H (the full method) is consistently slower than Base/Static+A/Dynamic+A on every model (e.g., 47.3s vs 40.6s for Deepseek-V3), and Appendix F.2 concedes it is 'constrained by higher runtime.' The main text nonetheless emphasizes efficiency parity, which is misleading.

Presentation is poor and in places internally inconsistent: the acronym alternates between TWNM and TWMN (Abstract vs. Section 3.2), there are numerous typos ('TooChain Retrieval', 'paramter', 'randomful tree structure', 'ike' for 'like'), the Appendix D generation prompt is garbled, several figures are low-resolution/illegible, and the Figure 5 caption ('Comparison of TSR Distribution') does not match the plotted content. These impede reproducibility.

No honest limitations section and no ethics/data-licensing discussion. The Conclusion only briefly gestures at 'remaining challenges'; there is no discussion of simulator validity, benchmark licensing, or the risk that graph-driven planning could systematically fail on genuinely unseen tool compositions.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: scaling LLM function-call agents to thousands of interdependent, continually evolving tools where step-by-step invocation without global awareness causes error accumulation.

The bilevel architecture (Section 3) is well-motivated and clearly separates high-level task reasoning (four-dimensional decision space: Direct Response, Intent Clarification, ToolChain Retrieval, Tool Execution) from low-level execution, which is a sensible decomposition.

The Tool World Navigation Model (TWNM) is technically reasonable: it combines structural (schema) and behavioral (usage) dependencies in a weighted HGT (Eq. 5), with a hybrid cross-entropy + adaptive-margin loss and a curriculum weighting schedule (Eq. 6-10). The adaptive margin that increases separation for high-weight edges is a nice touch.

The graph evolution mechanisms (incremental node integration, subgraph pruning Eq. 11, edge-weight propagation Eq. 12) explicitly target API drift/deprecation, aligning the representation with the stated challenge of continual updates.

Broad experimental evaluation across six model configurations (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-32B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, and fine-tuned Qwen2.5-14B), two benchmarks (ToolBench and API-Bank), and three difficulty levels, giving the results reasonable breadth.

Consistent relative gains over ReAct, ToolLLM, and α-UMI across models and difficulty levels while keeping execution steps close to the most efficient baseline (Table 1), supporting the efficiency claims.
The ablation (Table 2) progressively isolates Base → Static+A → Dynamic+A → Dynamic+H, showing that graph-based planning and heuristic search contribute measurable gains, especially on hard tasks.
The authors are reasonably transparent about the simulated nature of the evaluation and note remaining challenges in the conclusion.
weaknesses: The core evaluation is conducted in a simulated environment because 'real-time API execution is currently unavailable' (Section 4.1), using an LLM-based API simulator (Appendix E.3.3) that fabricates 'mock' outputs for novel APIs. Combined with an LLM judge (GPT-4.1, Appendix E.4.1), the entire pipeline is LLM-based, which risks circularity and may inflate absolute success rates. Real-world validity is only partially addressed by a small 60-query RapidAPI test (Appendix F.1), and it is unclear whether those calls were genuinely live.

The abstract claims TWNM integration 'boosts performance by up to 17 points on complex tasks,' but the tables show hard-task gains of about 13.8 points on DeepSeek-V3 (31.1 → 44.9) and ~6-7 points on Qwen2.5-14B/32B, so the headline number is not clearly supported by the reported evidence.

Algorithm 1 contains an internal inconsistency: the pseudocode updates beta as β = max(β, s × 1.15), whereas the text states β' = min(β, S_uv × 1.15) (correct for an upper bound). The alpha-pruning trigger (s < H(d) ∧ s < α) also mixes the dynamic threshold and the bound in a way that needs clarification.

Naming is inconsistent throughout (TWNM vs. TWMN in the abstract; figure labels such as 'toolchain_retrieval' and 'TooChain Retrieval'), and Appendix D (Data Generation) is garbled/unreadable, which hurts reproducibility of the task-construction pipeline.

The paper does not directly ablate the graph evolution mechanisms (incremental integration, pruning, edge propagation) nor the HGT design choices; link prediction quality is reported only as aggregate statistics in Table 8, so the claimed benefit of 'closed-loop evolution' is not quantitatively isolated.

The relationship between Table 1 and Table 2 is confusing: Table 1's NaviAgent corresponds to the non-SFT Dynamic+H variant, but this is not stated explicitly, and the finding that fine-tuned 14B (TSR 51.3) beats 32B (45.4) raises questions about data overlap, training set size (3,500+ examples), and fairness of the fine-tuning comparison.

The four-dimensional decision-space contribution is not isolated from the graph contribution: the Base configuration already includes the full decision agent, so the decision-space gains cannot be separated from the TWNM gains, and the analysis in Figure 5 is qualitative.

Some baseline comparisons are hard to interpret: α-UMI achieves higher TCR than NaviAgent in several Table 1 rows despite much lower TSR, and it is not discussed whether the baselines were tuned for this setting or given comparable graph information.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: scalable multi-tool orchestration under large and evolving API ecosystems.
Proposes a coherent bilevel architecture with a four-action planning space and a Tool World Navigation Model (TWNM) that jointly models structural and behavioral tool dependencies.
Provides extensive empirical evaluation on API-Bank, ToolBench, and 50 live RapidAPI endpoints, with consistent gains over several baselines across multiple backbone models and task difficulties.
Ablation studies isolate the contributions of the bilevel design, graph modeling, dynamic graph updates, and search strategies, supporting the claim that the components are complementary.
The graph evolution mechanisms (incremental node integration, pruning/reactivation, edge attribute propagation) are sensible for dynamic tool ecosystems and are partly evaluated in the appendix.
The appendix includes prompts, case studies, algorithm pseudocode, and graph maintenance overhead, which improves transparency to some extent.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely an engineering combination of existing ideas: tool graphs, HGT-based link prediction, planner-executor decomposition, and ReAct-style action spaces. The core novelty over prior graph-based tool planners is incremental.

Section 3.4 presents a theoretical result that is a standard KL projection onto a feasible action set. The proof is trivial, the theorem is not used to derive or improve the algorithm, and the section explicitly disclaims modeling the actual TWNM dynamics; it does not support the paper's central claims.

The evaluation metric for efficiency is problematic: Steps are counted only for successfully completed tasks. This biases comparisons across methods with different success rates, since methods that fail hard tasks early may appear more efficient.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are unclear. The paper does not sufficiently describe how baselines were reimplemented, prompted, or tuned across the different foundation models, making the reported gains difficult to fully attribute to the proposed method.

Key reproducibility details are missing or incomplete in the provided manuscript, including HGT training hyperparameters, negative sampling procedure, graph construction and link-prediction training data, and code/data availability. Appendix E.2 is referenced but not present or insufficient in the submitted text.

Link prediction performance is only moderate (AUC 0.71–0.75) and is not compared against link-prediction baselines. It is also unclear whether the model discovers genuinely unseen dependencies or largely reconstructs observed edges from the same invocation logs used to build the graph.

Real-world evaluation is limited to 50 APIs and 303 queries, which is small relative to the scalability claim. The paper does not rigorously test robustness under realistic API deprecation, version changes, or high-rate API drift beyond a small 50-query study.

Presentation has notable issues, including corrupted/typo text such as “Dynamic+Ally,” “TooChain,” and “ike,” malformed appendix examples, and unclear equations/algorithm details. The paper also lacks an explicit limitations section.
The main evaluation relies on LLM-based judging without human validation or inter-rater reliability, and no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported for the claimed gains.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: scalable multi-tool orchestration for LLM function-calling agents operating over large, changing tool ecosystems.

Integrates several components into a coherent system: a four-action bilevel planner, a heterogeneous graph (TWNM) over API/parameter nodes with an HGT link predictor, graph-search strategies, and feedback-driven graph maintenance.

Evaluation breadth is a genuine plus: two benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank) across multiple backbones (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-32B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o), plus a real-world study over 50 live RapidAPI endpoints and 303 queries.

Ablations (Tables 3, 4, 9, 11) reasonably isolate the contributions of the bilevel design, the tool graph, dynamic updates, search strategy, and specific decision actions (clarification, retrieval/execution decoupling).
Efficiency is reported alongside success (steps, runtime), and the paper documents maintenance overhead and provides case studies and pseudocode, aiding implementation.
weaknesses: The theoretical content (Section 3.4, Theorem 3.1, Proposition I.3) is a standard information-projection / KL-minimal restriction-and-renormalize result. The authors themselves concede it 'does not model how these sets are generated or updated' and does not 'fully characterize this entire TWNM-driven process.' It adds no modeling or algorithmic power and reads as mathematical padding rather than a contribution.

Evaluation validity is questionable for the central robustness claim. The reference call paths are simulated, and the API simulator is explicitly instructed to always return success ('Always "success" per operation'), so the main benchmark never genuinely exercises API failures, drift, or recovery, even though robustness to those is a headline claim. TSR is also LLM-judged against simulated references, which weakens the reported gains.

Mismatch between claims and evidence. The abstract/introduction foreground 'closed-loop evolution' (incremental node integration, edge-attribute propagation, pruning/reactivation) and 'path recombination' (I/O substitution, upstream rerouting, subgraph switching), yet these are evaluated only in a small appendix (F.2: 50 queries) or described but not directly measured. The scaling claim ('hundreds or thousands of tools') is asserted without systematic scaling curves or sensitivity to graph sparsity—the very limitation the paper attributes to prior work.

Moderate originality. Graph-based tool relations (ToolNet, ControlLLM), multi-action agent decision spaces, HGT link prediction, and alpha-beta/heuristic search are all pre-existing components; novelty lies mostly in recombination and engineering.

Reproducibility and presentation problems. Appendix D (data generation) is badly corrupted/garbled; the reference list contains multiple errors (EasyTool attributed to 'Yuan et al. (2020)' though 2024; the GA reference 'Shapiro et al. (2023)' is actually Shapiro 1999; GPT4Tools dated 2023 vs 2024; Xu et al. 2023 vs 2024); inconsistent labels appear ('TooChain Retrieval,' 'Dynamic+Ally'); and the training configuration is ambiguous (Table 1 reports Qwen2.5-14B at 35.8 TSR, which appears to be the non-SFT setting, while the method states Qwen2.5-14B is fine-tuned).

Hyperparameters are hand-set with no sensitivity analysis, e.g., the heuristic fitness weights (0.35/0.15/0.3/0.15/0.05), the alpha-beta thresholds (α0=0.4, β0=0.9), the annealing schedule, and the pruning/reactivation rate (10%). The basis for these choices is not justified.

Some headline numbers are hard to trace to the tables (e.g., the abstract's '13.1 points on complex tasks' from TWNM), and the graph construction relies on invocation logs whose provenance under a fresh environment is not clearly established, raising questions about how much of the gain stems from curated data versus the method itself.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and timely problem—scaling LLM function-call agents to hundreds/thousands of tools with unreliable or drifting APIs—and the bilevel decoupling of high-level action selection from graph-based toolchain construction is a sensible, well-motivated design.

Evaluation breadth is a real strength: five-plus backbones (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-32B, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o) across two benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank), plus an evaluation on 50 live RapidAPI endpoints spanning 7 domains and 303 queries, which is more practical validation than most tool-use papers provide.

The ablations (Table 3, Table 4) systematically isolate the contributions of the tool graph, dynamic graph updates, and the two search strategies (Alpha-Beta vs. heuristic), and the action-level ablation (Table 11) and pruning/reactivation study (Table 8) are informative.
Efficiency claims are supported: NaviAgent uses fewer steps and lower runtime than ToolNet, ToolPlanner, and α-UMI across models, so the gains are not simply bought with more computation.
weaknesses: Originality is limited. Link prediction over a heterogeneous tool graph (HGT), dynamic edge-weight updates, and planning/execution decoupling are each close to prior work the authors themselves cite (ToolNet's trajectory-based tool graph, ControlLLM's static dependency graphs, Tool-Planner's tool clusters). TWNM reads largely as a recombination of established components rather than a new mechanism.

The theoretical contribution (Sec. 3.4, Appendix I) is essentially a textbook result: the KL-minimal correction over context-dependent feasible sets is just restriction-and-renormalization (information projection). The authors concede it is 'intentionally modest,' and Theorem 3.1/I.2 plus the 'hard-rule' corollary add no new insight and feel like decorative padding.

Evaluation validity raises concerns. TSR is judged by an LLM (GPT-4.1) against reference chains, and most results come from a simulated API environment (Appendix E.3.3 'API Simulator'); combined with the small real-world set (50 APIs, 303 queries), the generalization claims ('robust under dynamic real-world conditions') are stronger than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility is weakened by underspecified data. The SFT set ('3,500+ examples sampled from our generated task set'), the generated dependency chains, and the graph-construction pipeline are not fully detailed, and several appendix sections are corrupted/garbled (e.g., the text in Appendix D, E.2/E.3 prompts), making faithful reproduction difficult.

Baseline comparability is questionable: α-UMI is a multi-LLM modular framework while NaviAgent is compared as a single backbone, and it is unclear whether baselines were tuned to comparable budgets, so some headline margins may be inflated.
Graph quality appears modest relative to the downstream claims: link-prediction AUC is only 0.71–0.75 (Table 10), yet the paper attributes large TSR gains to the graph.

Internal numeric consistency is not fully clear. For example, the SFT'd Qwen2.5-14B reportedly reaches 51.3% TSR while Qwen2.5-32B reaches only 45.4% (Table 4 vs Table 1), and the abstract's 'average gain of 13.1 points on complex tasks' is not directly traceable to a specific table.

Presentation contains numerous errors and artifacts ('TooChain Retrieval', 'Dynamic+Ally' embedded mid-text, garbled reference entries such as Tajbakhsh et al. and Rasley et al. that appear unrelated to the topic), which undermines confidence in the manuscript's care and readiness.
